blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Temperature: It is relative measure or indication of degree of hotness or coldness of a body. It is a scalar physical quantity with S.I. unit Kelvin (K).

Thermal equilibrium: Two bodies are said to be in thermal equilibrium, when no (net) heat flows from one body to the other i.e. when both the bodies are at the same temperature.

Thermometer: A thermometer is a device used to measure the temperature of a body.

Zeroth law of thermodynamics :  If objects A and B are separately in thermal equilibrium with a third object C (say thermometer), then objects A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other. Zeroth law of thermodynamics introduces the concept of temperature.

Different Scales of temperature

1.The Centigrade or Celsius scale (°C)

2.The Fahrenheit scale (°F)

3.Kelvin scale (K)

4. Relation b/w diff. scale (change in temp.)

$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{\Delta C}{5}=\frac{\Delta F}{9}=\frac{\Delta K}{5} \\ &  \Delta^{\circ} C=\Delta K \end{aligned} $

Relation between different scale (Temperature):

$\dfrac{C-0}{100}=\dfrac{F-32}{180}=\dfrac{K-273}{100}=\dfrac{A-L F P}{U F P-L F P}$

Absolute Zero: Equals to –273.15°C or 0 Kelvin (At this temperature kinetic energy of gas molecules becomes zero.)

blocks.question: At what temperature is the Fahrenheit scale reading equal to twice of Celsius?
blocks.answer: $\frac{F-32}{180}=\frac{C-0}{100} \Rightarrow \frac{2 x-32}{180}=\frac{x-0}{100} \Rightarrow x=160$

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: The temperature of an iron piece is raised from 30°C to 90°C. What is the change in its temperature on the Fahrenheit scale and on the Kelvin scale?
blocks.answer:
$\Delta \mathrm{C}=90^{\circ}-30^{\circ}=60^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

Temperature difference on Fahrenheit Scale

$\Delta \mathrm{F}=\dfrac{9}{5} \Delta \mathrm{C}=\dfrac{9}{5}\left(60^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)=108^{\circ} \mathrm{F}$

Temperature difference on Kelvin Scale

$\Delta \mathrm{K}=\Delta \mathrm{C}=60 \mathrm{~K}$

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
Common Mistakes

• Heat is often mistakenly treated as the same as temperature.
    • Sometimes, students use inconsistent or incorrect units, especially for specific heat capacity, latent heat, or temperature.
    • Mixing units like $\mathrm{J} / \mathrm{kg}{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ for specific heat capacity and $\mathrm{J} / \mathrm{C}^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ for heat capacity. can lead to incorrect results.

• Misunderstanding the sign conventions for heat exchange.
    • Ignoring or incorrectly interpreting the direction of heat flow between objects or systems.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Thermal Expansion: When matter is heated without any change in its state, it usually expands

Reason for Thermal expansion is assymetry in PE v/s $r$ curve

1. Linear Expansion:

Change in length is given as

$\Delta l=l_0 \propto \Delta T$

$\ell=\ell_0+\alpha \ell_0 \Delta \mathrm{~T}$

Unit of $\alpha$ is °C–1 or K–1.

2. Superficial (areal) expansion:

Percentage Change in area is given as

$\displaystyle \frac{\Delta A}{A} \times 100 \%$ = $\beta \Delta T \times 100\%$

$A=A_0+A_0 \beta \Delta T \quad \because \beta=2 \alpha$

3.Volume or cubical expansion:

Fractional change in volume is given as

$\displaystyle \frac{\Delta v}{V_0}=\gamma \Delta T$

$\mathrm{V}=\mathrm{V}_0(1+\gamma \Delta \mathrm{T})$ $\because \gamma=3 \alpha$

Note: coefficient of expansion for anisotropic material

$\gamma=\alpha_x+\alpha_y+\alpha_z \quad \beta=\alpha_x+\alpha_y$

Liquids have two coefficients of volume expansion:

Real & apparent volume expansion

$\displaystyle \gamma_{\text {real }}-3\alpha_{\text {vessel }}=\gamma_{\text {apparent }}$

$\gamma_r>3 \alpha_v \text{ level will rise} \\ \gamma_r<3 \alpha_v \text{ level will fall} \\ \gamma_r=3 \alpha_v \text{ level remain same}$

1.Co-efficient of apparent expansion : It is due to apparent (that appears to be, but is not) increase in the volume of liquid if expansion of vessel containing the liquid is not taken into account.

$\gamma_{\mathrm{a}}=\dfrac{\text { Apparent expansion in volume }}{\text { initial volume } \times \Delta \mathrm{T}}=\dfrac{(\Delta \mathrm{V})_{\mathrm{a}}}{\mathrm{~V} \times \Delta \mathrm{T}}$

2.Co-efficient of real expansion  : It is due to the actual increase in volume of liquid due to heating.

$\left.\gamma_{\mathrm{r}}=\dfrac{\text { Real increase in volume }}{\text { initial volume } \times \Delta \mathrm{T}}=\dfrac{(\Delta \mathrm{V})_{\mathrm{r}}}{\mathrm{~V} \times \Delta \mathrm{T}} \right\rvert\,$

Change in Density: $\rho=\rho_0(1-\gamma \Delta T)$

Anomalous behaviour of water: Generally, matter expands on heating and contracts on cooling. In case of water, it expands on heating if its temperature is greater than 4°C. In the range 0°C to 4°C, water contracts on heating and expands on cooling, i.e. $\gamma$  is negative. This behaviour of water in the range from 0°C to 4°C is called anomalous expansion.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Heat (Q): When two bodies at different temperature are made in contact, then net energy will flow from higher temperature body to lower temperature body, which is known as 'Heat'.

Calorie: The amount of heat needed to increase the temperature of 1g of water form 14.5°C to 15.5°C at a pressure of 1 atm is called 1 calorie.

$1 \text { calorie }=4.186 \text { Joule } \approx 4.2 \text { Joule }$

Mechanical Equivalent of Heat: According to Joule, work may be converted into heat and vice-versa. The ratio of work done to the heat produced is always constant.

$\dfrac{W}{Q}=\text { constant }=\mathrm{J} \Rightarrow \mathrm{~W}=\mathrm{JQ}$

Specific Heat (S or C): Amount of heat required to change the temperature of unit mass of substance by 1°C or 1K is called specific heat.

$\displaystyle S=\frac{Q}{m \Delta T}$

$\text { For ice } S_1=0.5~ \mathrm{cal} / \mathrm{g}-{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

$\text { for water } S_w=1~ \mathrm{cal} / \mathrm{g}-{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

$\text { for steam } S_s=0.5 ~\mathrm{cal} / \mathrm{g}-{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

$\text { Unit : SI :- joule/kg-K; CGS :- cal/g- }{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

$$1. Molar Specific Heat $\left(\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{mol}}\right)$:

$S_{\text {mol }}=\dfrac{Q}{\mu \Delta T}$

2. Gram Specific Heat (Sgram):

$S_{g \mathrm{ram}}=\dfrac{Q}{\mathrm{~m} \Delta \mathrm{~T}}$

Relation between Gram and Molar Specific heat

$\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{mol}}=\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{w}} \mathrm{~S}_{\mathrm{} \mathrm{gram}}$

Heat Capacity: Heat capacity of a body is defined as the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of a given mass of a body by 1°C or 1K. It is also called thermal capacity.

$\text { Heat capacity }=\dfrac{Q}{\Delta T}$

Dimension :[ ML2 T–2K–1]

Latent Heat / Hidden Heat: Heat required to change the state of unit mass depends on the nature of substance and is called latent heat of substance.

$\mathrm{L}=\dfrac{\mathrm{Q}}{\mathrm{~m}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{mL}$

1. Latent heat of fusion: It is the quantity of heat (in kilocalories) required to change 1 kg mass of a substance from solid to liquid state at its melting point.

$\left[\mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{mL}_{\mathrm{f}}\right]$

$L_f \text { for } \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}=80 \frac{\mathrm{cal}}{\mathrm{gm}}$

2. Latent heat of vaporization :The quantity of heat required (in Kilocalories) to change its 1 kg mass from liquid to vapour state at its boiling point.

$\mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{mLv}$

$L_v \text { for } \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}=540 \frac{\mathrm{cal}}{\mathrm{gm}}$

Heating Curve

Heating of Solid: If to a given mass (m) of a solid, heat is supplied at constant rate and a graph is plotted between temperature and heat, as shown in figure, it is called heating curve.

Assumptions for heating curve:

1. Initially object is in solid state and its temperature is less then melting point

2. Heat is given to the system by a constant power source.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Calorimetry

Principle of calorimetry: When two bodies at different temperatures are mixed, heat will be transferred from body at higher temperature to a body at lower temperature till both acquire same temperature.

Heat Lost = Heat Gained (Principle of calorimetry)

Principle of calorimetry represents the law of conservation of heat energy.

Law of Mixtures

$\begin{aligned} & \text { Heat given = heat absorbed } \\ & \mathrm{m}_1 \mathrm{~s}_1 \Delta \mathrm{~T}_1=\mathrm{m}_2 \mathrm{~s}_2 \Delta \mathrm{~T}_2 \\ & \mathrm{~m}_1 \mathrm{~s}_1\left(\mathrm{~T}_1-\mathrm{T}_{\operatorname{mix}}\right)=\mathrm{m}_2 \mathrm{~s}_2\left(\mathrm{~T}_{\mathrm{mix}}-\mathrm{T}_2\right) \\ & (\mathrm{s}=\text { specific heat }) \\ & \left(\mathrm{T}_1>\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{mix}}>\mathrm{T}_2\right) \end{aligned}$

Note: The temperature of mixture can never be lesser than lower temperature (as a body cannot be cooled below the temperature of cooling body) and greater than higher temperature (as a body cannot be heated above the temperature of heating body).

Water Equivalent: The water equivalent of a body is the amount of water (W in gram) that absorbs or gives out the same amount of heat as is done by the body when heated or cooled through same temperature

$\begin{aligned} &\begin{aligned} & \left(\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{c}}\right)_{\text {substance }}=\left(\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{C}}\right)_{\text {water }} \\ & \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{s}} \mathrm{~S}_{\mathrm{s}}=\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{W}} \mathrm{~S}_{\mathrm{W}} \\ & \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{s}} \mathrm{~S}_{\mathrm{s}}=\mathrm{W} \times 1 \mathrm{cal} / \mathrm{g}^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \end{aligned}\\ &\text { Water Equivalent = W in gram } \end{aligned}$

Geyser Problem:

$\begin{aligned} \text { Power } & =\frac{\text { Work }}{\text { Time }} \\ \text { Power }(P) & =\frac{\text { Heat }}{\text { Time }}(\because \text { Heat }(Q)=m s \Delta T) \\ \frac{P}{4.2} & =\frac{m s \Delta T}{t} \\ P & =\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\sec } \text { or watt } \quad \frac{\mathrm{J}}{\sec (4.2)}=\frac{\mathrm{Cal}}{\mathrm{sec}} \\ \frac{P}{4.2} & =\left(\frac{m}{t}\right) s \Delta T \\ \left(\frac{m}{t}\right) & =\text { Rate of flow of water in } \frac{\mathrm{g}}{\mathrm{~s}} \\ S_{\text {water }} & =1 \frac{\text { cal }}{\mathrm{g}{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}} \end{aligned}$

Change of States:

1. Melting: Conversion of solid into liquid state at constant temperature is known as melting.

2.Boiling: Evaporation within the whole mass of the liquid is called boiling.

3.Evaporation: Conversion of liquid into vapours at all temperatures is called evaporation.

4.Heat of evaporation: Heat required to change unit mass of a liquid into vapour at a given temperature is called heat of evaporation at that temperature.

5.Sublimation: Direct conversion of solid into vapour state is called sublimation.

6.Heat of sublimation: Heat required to change unit mass of solid directly into vapours at a given temperature is called heat of sublimation at that temperature.

7.Condensation: The process of conversion from gaseous or vapour state to liquid state is known as condensation.

8.Hoar frost: Direct conversion of vapours into solid is called hoar frost. This process is just reverse of the process of sublimation.

Phase: The phase of a substance is defined as its form which is homogeneous, physically distinct and mechanically separable from the other forms of that substance.

Phase Diagram for Water: A phase diagram of water is a graph in which pressure (P) is represented along the y–axis and temperature (T) is represented along the x-axis.

$\text{As } \\ \text{Pressure } \uparrow \text{ MP } \downarrow \text{ BP } \uparrow \\ \text{Pressure } \downarrow \text{ MP } \uparrow \text{ BP } \downarrow$

Triple Point of Water and Regelation: The three curves in the phase diagram of water meet at a single point A, which is called the triple point of water.

Triple point of water represents a unique condition, and it is used to define the absolute temperature.

Regelation: It is the melting of ice caused by pressure and its re-solidification when the pressure is removed.

Let the temperature of water in calorimeter is t.

Then heat lost by water = heat gained by calorimeter

$(0.1) \times 4200 \times(40-\mathrm{T})=100(\mathrm{~T}-30) $

$\Rightarrow 420 \times 40-420 \mathrm{~T}=100 \mathrm{~T}-3000 $

$\Rightarrow \mathrm{~T}=38.07^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

$\Rightarrow \dfrac{80}{100} \times \dfrac{10^3}{4.2}=100(1)\left(\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{f}}-10^{\circ}\right) \Rightarrow \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{f}}=11.9^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Modes of Heat Transfer: Heat is a form of energy which transfers from a body at higher temperature to a body at lower temperature. The transfer of heat from one body to another may take place by any one of the following modes.

1.Conduction: The process in which the material takes an active part by molecular action and energy is passed from one particle to another is called conduction. It is predominant in solids.

$\text { Rate of heat flow } i_T=\dfrac{d Q}{d t}=\dfrac{K A}{L}\left(T_1-T_2\right)$

1. Equivalent Thermal Conductivity in series Combination

$\begin{aligned} &\text { If lengths of rod is same then }\left(\mathrm{L}_1=\mathrm{L}_2=\mathrm{L}\right)\\ &\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{2 \mathrm{~K}_1 \mathrm{~K}_2}{\mathrm{~K}_1+\mathrm{K}_2} \end{aligned}$

$\displaystyle \begin{aligned} &\text { General formulae for series }\\ &K_{e 2}=\frac{l_1+l_2+\cdots}{\frac{l_1}{K_1}+\frac{l_2}{K_2}+\cdots} \end{aligned}$

2. Equivalent Thermal Conductivity in Parallel Combination

If Area of both rods are same then $ \left(\mathrm{A}_1=\mathrm{A}_2=\mathrm{A}\right)$

$\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{eq}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{K}_1+\mathrm{K}_2}{2}$

$\begin{aligned} &\text { General formulae for Parallel }\\ &k_{e q}=\frac{K_1 A_1+K_2 A_2+\cdots \cdot}{A_1+A_2+\cdots} \end{aligned}$

Temperature of junction: When we have to calculate the temperature of junction then we equate the rate of heat flow from both parts

$\mathrm{T}_0=\dfrac{\mathrm{K}_1 \mathrm{~L}_2 \mathrm{~T}_1+\mathrm{K}_2 \mathrm{~L}_1 \mathrm{~T}_2}{\mathrm{~K}_1 \mathrm{~L}_2+\mathrm{K}_2 \mathrm{~L}_1}$

Growth of Ice on Lake: time taken by ice to grow a thickness x is

$\mathrm{t}=\dfrac{\rho \mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{KT}} \int_0^{\mathrm{x}} \mathrm{xdx}=\dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{\rho \mathrm{~L}}{\mathrm{KT}} \mathrm{x}^2$

Time taken to double and triple the thickness ratio  $t_1: t_2: t_3:: 1^2: 2^2: 3^2$

Ratio of time taken to form thickness

$(0 \rightarrow \mathrm{x}):(\mathrm{x} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{x}):(2 \mathrm{x} \rightarrow 3 \mathrm{x})$

$\Delta \mathrm{t}_1: \Delta \mathrm{t}_2: \Delta \mathrm{t}_3:: \\ \left(\mathrm{x}^2-0^2\right):\left(2 \mathrm{x}^2-\mathrm{x}^2\right):\left(3 \mathrm{x}^2-2 \mathrm{x}^2\right)$

$\Delta \mathrm{t}_1: \Delta \mathrm{t}_2: \Delta \mathrm{t}_3: 1: 3: 5 $

2. Convection: The transfer of energy by actual motion of particle of medium from one place to another is called convection. It is predominant is fluids (liquids and gases).

• Reason for convection is difference in density due to heating
    • Direction of convection is bottoms to top due to gravity.

3. Radiation: Quickest way of transmission of heat is known as radiation. In this mode of energy transmission, heat is transferred from one place to another without effecting the intervening medium.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: Ice starts freezing in a lake with water at 0°C when the atmospheric temperature is −10°C. If the time taken for 1cm of ice to be formed is 12min, the time taken for the thickness of the ice to change from 1 to 2cm will be
blocks.answer:
Time taken by ice to grow a thickness,

$t=\dfrac{e L}{2 K T} x^2$

Hence time interval to change thickness from 0 to y, from y to 2y and so on will be in the ratio.

$\begin{aligned} & \Delta \mathrm{t}_1: \Delta \mathrm{t}_2: \Delta \mathrm{t}_3=\left(1^2-0^2\right):\left(2^2-1^2\right):\left(3^2-2^2\right) \\ & \Delta \mathrm{t}_1: \Delta \mathrm{t}_2: \Delta \mathrm{t}_3=1: 3: 5 \end{aligned}$

$\Delta \mathrm{t}_2=3 \Delta \mathrm{t}_1=3 \times 12=36 \mathrm{~min} .$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Prevost's Theory: According to Prevost's Theory, at every possible temperature (except zero kelvin temperature) there is a continuous heat energy exchange between a body and its surrounding and this exchange carry on for infinite time.

1.When a cold body is placed in the hot surrounding

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{B}}<\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{S}} \\ & \mathrm{Q}_{\text {emission }}<\mathrm{Q}_{\text {absorption }} \end{aligned}$

2.When a hot body placed in cooler surrounding

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{B}}>\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{S}} \\ & \mathrm{Q}_{\text {emission }}>\mathrm{Q}_{\text {absorption }} \end{aligned}$

3.When the temperature of a body is equal to the temperature of the surrounding

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{B}}=\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{S}} \\ & \mathrm{Q}_{\text {emission }}=\mathrm{Q}_{\text {absorotion }} \end{aligned}$

Absorptive power or absorptive coefficient (a) : The ratio of amount of radiation absorbed by a surface (Qa) to the amount of radiation incident (Q) upon it, is defined as the coefficient of absorption. It is unitless and dimensionless.

$a=\frac{Q_a}{Q} $

Spectral absorptive power:

$a_\lambda=\frac{Q_{a_\lambda}}{Q_\lambda}$

a= $\int_0^{\infty} \mathrm{a}_\lambda \mathrm{~d} \lambda $. For ideal black body  $ \mathrm{a}_{\lambda}$ and a=1, a and  $\mathrm{a}_{\lambda} $ are unitless

Emissive power (E):  The amount of heat radiation emitted by unit surface area in unit second at a particular temperature.

$E_{G B}=\frac{Q_{G B}}{A t} ; \quad E_{I B B}=\frac{Q_{I B B}}{A t}$

SI unit: J/m2–s or Watt/m2

Emissivity (e)

Absolute emissivity or emissivity: Radiation energy given out by a unit surface area of a body in unit time corresponding to unit temperature difference w.r.t. the surroundings is called Emissivity.

SI Unit:  W/m2

$\text { Relative emissivity ( } \left.e_r\right) \text { : } e_r=\frac{E_{G B}}{E_{I B B}}=\dfrac{\text { emitted radiation by gray body }\left(Q_{G B}\right)}{\text { emitted radiation by ideal bladk body }\left(Q_{I B B}\right)}$

GB = Gray or General body, IBB = Ideal black body

(1) Unitless

(2) For ideal black body ; er = 1

(3) range ; 0 < er < 1

Ideal Black Body: A body which absorbs all thermal radiations falling at its surface at low temperature and emits out all these absorbed radiations at high temperature, irrespective of their wave length is known as an ideal black body.

Kirchhoff's Law: At a given temperature for all bodies the ratio of their emissive power (E) to absorptive power (a) is constant and this constant is equal to emissive power (EiBB) of the ideal black body at same temperature.

$\dfrac{E_{\mathrm{GB}}}{\mathrm{a}}=\mathrm{E}_{I \mathrm{BB}}$

Good absorbers are Good emitters and Bad absorbers are Bad emitters.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Stefan's Law: The amount of radiation emitted per second per unit area (E) by ideal black body is directly proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature (T).

$\mathrm{E} \propto \mathrm{~T}^4 \Rightarrow \mathrm{E_{IBB}}=\sigma \mathrm{T}^4$

$E_{G B}=e_r \sigma T^4$

Newton's Law of Cooling: This law states that the rate of temperature change of an object is directly proportional to the difference in temperature between the object and its environment.

$-\frac{d T}{d t}=-k\left(T-T_{\mathrm{0}}\right)$

For Numerical Problems (Newton's Law of cooling)

$\left[\frac{\mathrm{T}_1-\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{t}}\right]=\mathrm{K}\left[\frac{\mathrm{~T}_1+\mathrm{T}_2}{2}-\mathrm{T}_0\right]$

Spectral Emissive Power : The amount of heat radiation emitted by unit area of the body in one second in unit spectral region at a given wavelength.

$\begin{array}{ll} \text { For } \mathrm{GB}, \mathrm{E}_\lambda=\frac{\left(\mathrm{Q}_{\lambda, \dot{A}}\right)_{\mathrm{GB}}}{\mathrm{At}} & \\ \text { For IBB, } \mathrm{E}_\lambda=\frac{\left(\mathrm{Q}_{\lambda \dot{A}}\right)_{\mathrm{IBB}}}{\mathrm{At}} \\ \text { UNIT : SI } \rightarrow \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^2-\AA \end{array}$

If the temperature of a black body is increased, the wavelength corresponding to maximum emission of radiation is shifted from longer wavelength to shorter wavelength, due to this colour of the body changes.

$\mathrm{T}_3>\mathrm{T}_2>\mathrm{T}_1 ; \lambda_{\mathrm{m}_3}<\lambda_{\mathrm{m}_2}<\lambda_{\mathrm{m}_1}$

Wein's Displacement Law: The wavelength (λm) corresponding to maximum emission of radiation decrease with increasing temperature. This is known as Wein’s displacement law.

$\lambda_{\mathrm{m}} \propto \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{~T}} \Rightarrow \lambda_{\mathrm{m}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{b}}{\mathrm{~T}}$

$\text { For numerical } \Rightarrow \lambda_{\mathrm{m}} \mathrm{~T}=\mathrm{b}$

$\text { (where, } \mathrm{b} \text { is Wein's constant }=2.89 \times 10^{-3}~ \mathrm{meter ~ Kelvin(mK)} \text { ) }$

$\lambda_{\mathrm{m}_1} \mathrm{~T}_1=\lambda_{\mathrm{m}_2} \mathrm{~T}_2$

Solar Constant: The Sun emits radiant energy continuously in space of which an in significant part reaches the Earth. The solar radiant energy received per unit area per unit time by a black surface held at right angles to the Sun's rays and placed at the mean distance of the Earth (in the absence of atmosphere) is called solar constant. The solar constant S is taken for earth to be 1340 watt/m2

$\left.\mathrm{S}=\dfrac{\sigma \mathrm{T}^2 \mathrm{R}^2}{\mathrm{~d}^2} \Rightarrow \mathrm{~S} \propto \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{~d}^2} \Rightarrow \dfrac{\mathrm{~S}_{\text {planet }}}{\mathrm{S}_{\text {earth }}}=\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{e}}}{\mathrm{~d}_{\mathrm{p}}}\right)^2 \right\rvert\,$

Temperature of Sun-$5732 \mathrm{~K}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Kinetic Energy of Gas: All molecules of gas are continuously performing motion in random direction or say zig-zag direction. Apart from translational motion these molecules also perform rotational as well as vibrational motion. Thus, these molecules have kinetic energy associated with these motions. It is dependent on absolute temperature. Increasing temperature increases kinetic energy of gas.

Potential Energy: Intermolecular attraction force exists between molecules and thus every molecules have some potential energy.

Greater Intermolecular force (IMF), lesser will be potential energy and greater will be magnitude of potential energy

(1) Intermolecular force: Solid > Liquid > Gas (Real) > Ideal Gas (IMF = 0)

(2) Potential Energy: Solid < Liquid <= Gas (Real) < Ideal Gas (IMF = 0)

Internal Energy of Gas: Internal energy of gas is defined as sum of potential energy and kinetic energy at a temperature.

(1)Internal kinetic energy : Same for all

(2) Internal potential Energy : Maximum for ideal gas (PE = 0) and Minimum for solids (PE = negative)

(3)Internal Energy : Maximum for Ideal gas and Minimum for solid

Moles of gas ,$\mu=\frac{M}{M_w}=\frac{N}{N_A} \,$

Avogadro constant , $\mathrm{N}_A=6.023 \times 10^{23} \frac{\text { molecules }}{\text { mole }}$

Universal gas constant , $ \mathrm{R}=8.31 \frac{\mathrm{~J}}{\mathrm{~mole}-\mathrm{K}} \approx 2 \frac{\mathrm{cal}}{\mathrm{~mole}-\mathrm{K}}$

Specific gas constant , $ r=\frac{R}{M_w}$

Boltzmann constant , $ \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{b}}=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{~N}_{\mathrm{A}}}=1.38 \times 10^{-23} \frac{\mathrm{~J}}{\mathrm{~K}}$

Ideal Gas: A gas which follows all gas laws and gas equation at every possible temperature and pressure is known as ideal or perfect gas.

$\begin{aligned} & P V=\mu R T \\ & P V=\frac{M}{M_w} R T \quad \Rightarrow  P V=\left[\frac{m \mathrm{~N}}{\mathrm{mN}_{\mathrm{A}}}\right] \mathrm{RT} \\ & \mathrm{PV}=\left[\frac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{~N}_{\mathrm{A}}}\right] \mathrm{NT} \Rightarrow \mathrm{PV}=\mathrm{Nk}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{~T} \\ & \mathrm{P}=\frac{\rho \mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{W}}} \end{aligned}$

$\dfrac{P}{\rho}=\dfrac{R T}{M_w}=\dfrac{K_b T}{m}$

Gas Laws

1. Charle's Law:

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{V} \propto \mathrm{~T} \quad \text { (m and } \mathrm{P} \text { are Constant) } \\ & \frac{\mathrm{V}_1}{\mathrm{~V}_2}=\frac{\mathrm{T}_1}{\mathrm{~T}_2} \end{aligned}$

2. Boyle's Law:

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{V} \propto \frac{1}{\mathrm{P}} \quad \text { (m and } \mathrm{T} \text { are Constant) } \\ & \mathrm{P}_1 \mathrm{~V}_1=\mathrm{P}_2 \mathrm{~V}_2 \end{aligned}$

3. Gay–Lussac's Law:

$\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{P} \propto \mathrm{~T} \quad \text { ( } \mathrm{m} \text { and } \mathrm{V} \text { are Constant) }\\ &\frac{\mathrm{P}_1}{\mathrm{P}_2}=\frac{\mathrm{T}_1}{\mathrm{~T}_2} \end{aligned}$

4. Avogadro's Law: According to this law, at same temperature and pressure, equal volume of all gases contain equal number of molecules, i.e., N1 = N2 if P, V and T are same.

5. Dalton's Partial Pressure Mixture Law: According to this law, the pressure exerted by mixture of non-reactive gases is equal to the sum of partial pressure of each component gases present in the mixture.

$P=P_1+P_2+P_3 \ldots$

Partial pressure of gas 1

$P_1=\frac{\mu_1}{\mu_T} \times P_T$

Average velocity: Because molecules are in random motion in all possible direction with all possible velocity. Therefore, the average velocity of the gas molecules in container is zero.

$\langle\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}\rangle=\frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_1+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_2+\ldots \ldots \ldots . . . \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{N}}}{\mathrm{~N}}=0$

Average speed or Mean speed (vavg)

$<|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}|>\equiv \mathrm{v}_{\text {mean }} \equiv \mathrm{v}_{\text {avg }}=\frac{\left|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_1\right|+\left|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_2\right|+\ldots \ldots \ldots . .\left|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{n}}\right|}{\mathrm{N}}$

Most probable speed (vmp): At a given temperature, the speed to which maximum number of molecules belongs is called as most probable speed (vmp)

RMS Speed (vrms): RMS Speed (root mean squared speed) is equal to square root of the sum of square of speed of each molecule of a gas.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\mathrm{v}_1^2+\mathrm{v}_2^2+\mathrm{v}_3^2 \ldots \ldots \ldots \ldots+\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{n}}^2}{\mathrm{~N}}}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Maxwell's law of distribution of velocities :Maxwell had drawn a curve between number of molecules, moving with a particular velocity, and velocity of molecules known as velocity distribution curve.

Pressure of An Ideal gas:$P=\frac{1}{3} \rho v_{\mathrm{rms}}^2$

Translational Kinetic Energy:

​$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{T}}=\frac{3}{2} \mathrm{PV}=\frac{1}{2} m_{\text {total }} v_{\text {rms }}^2 \\ & \frac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{T}}}{\mathrm{~V}}=\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{V}}=\text { Energy density } \\ & \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{V}}=\frac{3}{2} \mathrm{P} \end{aligned}$

Expression of RMS Speed

$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{P}}{\rho}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{w}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{~m}}}$

(1)If gas is same ($M_w = \text{const.}$) and temp. is changed

$V_{\text{rms}} \propto \sqrt{T}$

(2) If temperature is constant and gas is changed

$V_{\text{rms}} \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{M_w}}$

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{P}}{\rho}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{w}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{~m}}}$

$v_{\mathrm{mp}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{P}}{\rho}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{w}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{~m}}}$

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{av}}=\sqrt{\frac{8 \mathrm{P}}{\pi \rho}}=\sqrt{\frac{8 \mathrm{RT}}{\pi \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{w}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{8 \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{~T}}{\pi \mathrm{~m}}}$

$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{rms}}>\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{Mean}}>\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{MP}}$

(3) If pressure changed at constant temp. No effect on  $V_{rms}$ .

(4) $V_{rms}$ doesn't depend on pressure but pressure depends on  $V_{rms}$ .

Escape Velocity: The minimum velocity required for which molecule or object to escape out from earth surface.

$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{es}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{GM}}{\mathrm{R}}} \\  \Rightarrow \left(\mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{es}}\right)_{\mathrm{earth}}=11.2 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{sec}$

Relation of escape Velocity with rms

Condition for atmosphere to be present at the surface of any planet:

Vrms < Ves $\rightarrow$Atmosphere present

Vrms ≥ Ves $\rightarrow$ No atmosphere

$\mathrm{T}_{\min }=\dfrac{\left(\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{es}}\right)^2 \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{w}}}{3 \mathrm{R}} \quad \text{OR } \quad T_{\text {min }}=\dfrac{M_w}{2} \times 10^7 \mathrm{~K}$  $(M_w ~ in~ Kg)$

Note:

(1)   If we continuously increase the temperature at 104 K hydrogen gas molecules will leave the earth surface first.

(2) Moon has no atmosphere because there rms speed of gas molecules is greater then the escape velocity.

blocks.title: Core concepts
blocks.text:
Degrees of Freedom (f): The number of independent ways in which a molecule or an atom can exhibit motion or have energy is called its degrees of freedom.

Types of Degrees of freedom:

(a) Translational Degree of freedom : Number of independent ways in which a gas molecule may perform translatory motion. There are maximum three degree of freedom corresponding to translational motion.

(b) Rotational Degree of freedom : Number of independent ways in which a gas molecule may perform rotational motion. The number of degrees of freedom in this case depends on the structure of the molecule.

(c) Vibrational Degree of freedom : Number of independent ways in which a gas molecule may vibrate. It is exhibited at high temperature only.

Maxwell's Law of Equipartition of Energy: The total kinetic energy of a gas molecules is equally distributed among its all degree of freedom and the energy associated with each degree of freedom at absolute temperature T is $\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{~T}$

Mayer’s Law:

$C_p-C_v=R$

$\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{v}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{f}}{2} \mathrm{R} ; \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{p}}=\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{f}}{2}+1\right) \mathrm{R}$

Molar specific heat for mixture of gases:

$Q_{\text {mix }}=Q_1+Q_2$

$C_{\operatorname{mix}}=\dfrac{\mu_1 C_1+\mu_2 C_2}{\mu_1+\mu_2}$

$\left(\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{V}}\right)_{\text {mix }}=\dfrac{\mu_1 \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{v}_1}+\mu_2 \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{V}_2}}{\mu_1+\mu_2}$

$\left(\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{P}}\right)_{\text {mix }}=\dfrac{\mu_1 \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{P}_1}+\mu_2 \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{P}_2}}{\mu_1+\mu_2}$

$\gamma_{\text {mix }}=\dfrac{\mu_1 C_{p_1}+\mu_2 C_{P_2}}{\mu_1 C_{v_1}+\mu_2 C_{V_2}}$

Mixture of Gases

Case – I: Here two gases kept in two different vessels are mixed in another vessel

$\dfrac{P_1 V_1}{T_1}+\dfrac{P_2 V_2}{T_2}=\dfrac{P_3 V_3}{T_3}$

Case – II: Here two gases kept in two different vessels connected via a tube as shown. Cross-section area of this tube is very small so its volume can be neglected w.r.t. volume of vessel

$\dfrac{\mathrm{P}_1 \mathrm{~V}_1}{\mathrm{~T}_1}+\dfrac{\mathrm{P}_2 \mathrm{~V}_2}{\mathrm{~T}_2}=\dfrac{P V_1}{\mathrm{~T}_1^{\prime}}+\dfrac{\mathrm{PV}_2}{\mathrm{~T}_2^{\prime}}$

Mean Free Path: The average distance travelled by a molecule between two successive collisions is called as mean free path  of the molecule.

$ \lambda_{\mathrm{m}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2} \pi \mathrm{~d}^2 \mathrm{n}} $

Here,

$ \mathrm{n}  =\dfrac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{~V}}= $ No. of molecules per unit volume

$ \mathrm{d}  =\text { diameter of a molecule } $

Compressibility Factor: It is used to express the extent of deviation of a real gas from ideal gas behaviour. It is denoted by Z.

Case-I :         Z = 1      $\Rightarrow$           [Vreal = Videal]

Thus, real gas behaves as ideal gas (zero deviation).

Case-II :         Z > 1     $\Rightarrow$          [Vreal > Videal]

Thus, real gas expand with respect to ideal gas and hence we can say positive deviation.

Case-III :       Z < 1       $\Rightarrow$         [Vreal < Videal]

Thus, real gas compress with respect to ideal gas and hence we can say negative deviation.

Real Gas : Practically, no gas is ideal at all. They show some deviation from ideal gas behaviour and are known as Real gas.

Main cause of deviation is two postulates that have been assumed in Kinetic Theory of Gases :-

(1) Interaction force between gas molecules are considered negligible

(2) Size of Gas molecules is considered negligible but practically they are not negligible.

Compressibility Factor Curve:

NOTE: Real gas approaches ideal gas behaviour at Low Pressure and High Temperature(Low Density).

Vander Waal's Equation for Real Gas

Pressure Correction: Since, we have neglected intermolecular interaction, thus actual pressure of gas will be less than ideal pressure.

$P_{\text {ideal }}=P_{\text {real }}+\dfrac{\mu^2 a}{V^2}$

Volume Correction: Also, we have neglected size of molecules but actual volume occupied by real gas will be

$\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{V}_{\text {ideal }}=\mathrm{V}_{\text {real }}-\mu \mathrm{b}\\ &\mathrm{b} \rightarrow \text { Constant and value depends on real gas} \end{aligned}$

$\left(P+\dfrac{\mu^2 a}{V^2}\right)(V-\mu b)=\mu R T $

blocks.text:
Thermodynamic System: The system which can be represented in terms of pressure (P), volume (V) and temperature (T), is known thermodynamic system

  • Surroundings-Anything outside the System that exchanges energy with the System and tends to change its properties is called its surroundings.
  • Universe-The system and its surroundings are together known as the universe.
  • Boundary-Real or imaginary wall that separates the system from the surroundings
Types of Systems:

(1) Open System - Any interaction is possible.

(2) Closed System - Impenetrable by matter, but other  interactions can occur.

(3) Isolated System - No interactions can occur.

• Intensive - Independent of the size (or mass) of the system. Example:- pressure, temperature, etc.

  • Extensive-depends on the size (or mass) of the system. Example:-volume, number of moles, etc.
Thermodynamic variables of the system :

  • Composition (m)
  • Temperature (T)
  • Volume (V)
  • Pressure (P)
  • Mass

blocks.title: Work Done by Thermodynamic System
blocks.text:
• If pressure of gas inside the cylinder having piston $=P$
  • Then the force on the piston due to gas is $F=PA$
  • When the piston is pushed outward an infinitesimal distance $dx$ by the gas
  • The work done by the gas is $dW=F \times dx=PA dx$
  • The change in volume of the gas is $dV=Adx,\therefore \mathrm{dW}=\mathrm{PdV}$
  • For a finite change in volume from $V_i ~to ~V_f$,this equation is then integrated between $V_i ~to ~V_f$ to find the net work done
$\displaystyle W=\int_{V_I}^{V_f} d W=\int_{V_i}^{V_f} F d V$

Hence "the work done by a gas is equal to the area under $P-V $ graph"

Case :$1^{s t}$ $W_{\text {A~to B }}=+ \text { (Area shaded) }$

Case:$2^{n d}$ $W_{\text {A~to~B }}=- \text { (Area shaded) }$

Explanation: Asking about the work done for given process equation.

Given that:

$V_{\text {initial }}=1 \mathrm{~m}^3, V_{\text {final }}=4 \mathrm{~m}^3$

Calculation :

$\displaystyle P = \frac{100}{V^{1/2}}$

$W=200[2 -1]$

modules.name: Thermodynamic Process And Law of Thermodynamics

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Process: When a system changes from one equilibrium state to another, the path of successive states through which the system passes is called a process.

  • Cyclic Process-It is a thermodynamic process in which the system returns to its initial stage after undergoing a series of changes.
  • Non–cyclic process-It is a process in which the system does not return to its initial stage.
  • Quasi–static or equilibrium process-It A thermodynamic process that occurs very slowly, ensuring that at every moment, the temperature and pressure remain uniform throughout the system, is referred to as a quasi-static process..
First Law of Thermodynamics(FLOT): Suppose some heat is supplied to a system capable of doing external work. In that case, the heat absorbed by the system is equivalent to the combined effect of the increase in its internal energy and the external work it executes.

$\Delta Q=\Delta U+\Delta \mathrm{W}$

  • Mathematical Method $\mathrm{W}=\int_{V_i}^{V_f} P d V$
  • Cyclic Process-:Work =Area of the closed curve in PV Graph
  • Isochoric Process :Work =0
  • Isothermal Process: $\text { Work }=\mu R T \log _e\left[\frac{V_f}{V_i}\right]=\mu R T \log _e\left[\frac{P_i}{P_f}\right]$
  • Adiabatic Process :$\text { Work }=\mu R \frac{\left(T_f-T_i\right)}{1-\gamma}$
  • Isobaric Process:$\text { Work= } \mathrm{P}\left(V_f-V_i\right)=\mu R\left(T_f-T_i\right) \mid$
6.  Polytropic Process:$\text { Work }=\dfrac{\mu R\left(T_f-T_i\right)}{1-x}$

Graphical method $\Delta \mathbf{W}$= Area enclosed between PV curve and Volume axis.

Cyclic Process: A cyclic process in thermodynamics refers to a process in which a system undergoes a series of changes but eventually returns to its original state.

1. Isometric or Isochoric Process: Isochoric process is a thermodynamic process that takes place at constant volume of the system, but pressure and temperature varies for change in state of the system.

Volume= Constant

$\text { Equation of state } \Rightarrow \frac{P}{T}=\text { constant }$

$\text { Work done } \mathrm{W}=\int P d V=0 \quad(: \mathrm{dV}=0)$

$\text { Form of First Law }, \mathrm{Q}=\Delta U=\mu C_v \Delta T$

$\text { Slope of the P-V curve } \dfrac{d P}{d V}=\infty$

$\text { Bulk Modulus }=\beta=-\frac{d P}{d V / v}=-v \frac{d P}{d v}=\infty$

2. Isobaric Process: Isobaric process is a thermodynamic process that takes place at constant pressure, but volume and temperature varies for change in state of the system.

Pressure = constant

$\displaystyle \text { Equation of state } \Rightarrow \frac{V}{T}=\text { constant }(\mathrm{V} \propto \mathrm{~T})$

$\displaystyle \text { Work done } \mathrm{}=\mathrm{W}=\int_{V_i}^{V_f} P d V=\mathrm{P}\left(V_f-V_i\right)$

From the FLOT : $\Delta Q=\Delta U+W$

$\mu~C_p\left(T_f-T_i\right)=\mu C_v\left(T_f-T_i\right)+\mathrm{P}\left(V_f-V_i\right)$

$\text { Slope of the PV curve }\left(\dfrac{d P}{d V}\right)_{\text {isobaric }}=0$

$\text{Bulk Modulus  } \beta_{IB}=0 $

3. Isothermal Process: In this process pressure and volume of system change but temperature remains constant.

Temperature= constant

Equation of state PV=Constant

$\text { Work done } \mathrm{W}=\mu R T \log _e\left[\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}\right\rfloor=2.303 \mu R T \log _{10}\left\lfloor\dfrac{P_1}{P_2}\right\rfloor$

$\text { Form of First Law } \Delta U=0$ so that $\Delta Q=W_{\text {isothermal }}$

$\text { Slope of isothermal curve } \left.\left[\dfrac{d P}{d V}\right]_{\text {isothermal }}=-\dfrac{P}{V}\right\rfloor$

Bulk modulus ${\beta _{IT}} = P$

4. Adiabatic Process: It is that thermodynamic process in which pressure, volume and temperature of the system do change but there is no exchange of heat between the system and the surroundings.

$\text{Adiabatic equation on of state} \\  \begin{aligned} & P V^\gamma=C \\ & T V^{\gamma-1}=C \\ & T^\gamma P^{1-\gamma}=C \end{aligned}$

No heat exchange between system and surroundings.

$\text { Work done } \mathrm{W}=\dfrac{1}{\gamma-1}\left[P_1 V_1-P_2 V_2\right]=\dfrac{\mu R}{\gamma-1}\left(T_1-T_2\right)$

$\text { Slope of adiabatic curve }\left[\dfrac{d P}{d V}\right]_{\text {adiabatic }}=\dfrac{-\Upsilon P}{V}$

$\text{Bulk Modulus } =\beta_{A D}=\gamma P$

5.Polytropic Process

$\mathrm{P} V^x=\text { Constant }, \mathrm{C}=C_v+\dfrac{R}{1-x}$

$\text { For isobaric } \mathrm{x}=0, \mathrm{C}=C_P=\dfrac{R}{\gamma-1}+\mathrm{R}=C_v+R$

$\text { For isothermal } x=1, C=\infty$

$\text { For adiabatic } x=\gamma, C=0$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Thermal Expansion: When matter is heated without any change in its state, it usually expands

Reason for Thermal expansion is assymetry in PE v/s $r$ curve

1. Linear Expansion:

Change in length is given as

$\Delta l=l_0 \propto \Delta T$

$\ell=\ell_0+\alpha \ell_0 \Delta \mathrm{~T}$

Unit of $\alpha$ is °C–1 or K–1.

2. Superficial (areal) expansion:

Percentage Change in area is given as

$\displaystyle \frac{\Delta A}{A} \times 100 \%$ = $\beta \Delta T \times 100\%$

$A=A_0+A_0 \beta \Delta T \quad \because \beta=2 \alpha$

3.Volume or cubical expansion:

Fractional change in volume is given as

$\displaystyle \frac{\Delta v}{V_0}=\gamma \Delta T$

$\mathrm{V}=\mathrm{V}_0(1+\gamma \Delta \mathrm{T})$ $\because \gamma=3 \alpha$

Note: coefficient of expansion for anisotropic material

$\gamma=\alpha_x+\alpha_y+\alpha_z \quad \beta=\alpha_x+\alpha_y$

Liquids have two coefficients of volume expansion:

Real & apparent volume expansion

$\displaystyle \gamma_{\text {real }}-3\alpha_{\text {vessel }}=\gamma_{\text {apparent }}$

$\gamma_r>3 \alpha_v \text{ level will rise} \\ \gamma_r<3 \alpha_v \text{ level will fall} \\ \gamma_r=3 \alpha_v \text{ level remain same}$

1.Co-efficient of apparent expansion : It is due to apparent (that appears to be, but is not) increase in the volume of liquid if expansion of vessel containing the liquid is not taken into account.

$\gamma_{\mathrm{a}}=\dfrac{\text { Apparent expansion in volume }}{\text { initial volume } \times \Delta \mathrm{T}}=\dfrac{(\Delta \mathrm{V})_{\mathrm{a}}}{\mathrm{~V} \times \Delta \mathrm{T}}$

2.Co-efficient of real expansion  : It is due to the actual increase in volume of liquid due to heating.

$\left.\gamma_{\mathrm{r}}=\dfrac{\text { Real increase in volume }}{\text { initial volume } \times \Delta \mathrm{T}}=\dfrac{(\Delta \mathrm{V})_{\mathrm{r}}}{\mathrm{~V} \times \Delta \mathrm{T}} \right\rvert\,$

Change in Density: $\rho=\rho_0(1-\gamma \Delta T)$

Anomalous behaviour of water: Generally, matter expands on heating and contracts on cooling. In case of water, it expands on heating if its temperature is greater than 4°C. In the range 0°C to 4°C, water contracts on heating and expands on cooling, i.e. $\gamma$  is negative. This behaviour of water in the range from 0°C to 4°C is called anomalous expansion.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Heat (Q): When two bodies at different temperature are made in contact, then net energy will flow from higher temperature body to lower temperature body, which is known as 'Heat'.

Calorie: The amount of heat needed to increase the temperature of 1g of water form 14.5°C to 15.5°C at a pressure of 1 atm is called 1 calorie.

$1 \text { calorie }=4.186 \text { Joule } \approx 4.2 \text { Joule }$

Mechanical Equivalent of Heat: According to Joule, work may be converted into heat and vice-versa. The ratio of work done to the heat produced is always constant.

$\dfrac{W}{Q}=\text { constant }=\mathrm{J} \Rightarrow \mathrm{~W}=\mathrm{JQ}$

Specific Heat (S or C): Amount of heat required to change the temperature of unit mass of substance by 1°C or 1K is called specific heat.

$\displaystyle S=\frac{Q}{m \Delta T}$

$\text { For ice } S_1=0.5~ \mathrm{cal} / \mathrm{g}-{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

$\text { for water } S_w=1~ \mathrm{cal} / \mathrm{g}-{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

$\text { for steam } S_s=0.5 ~\mathrm{cal} / \mathrm{g}-{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

$\text { Unit : SI :- joule/kg-K; CGS :- cal/g- }{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

$$1. Molar Specific Heat $\left(\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{mol}}\right)$:

$S_{\text {mol }}=\dfrac{Q}{\mu \Delta T}$

2. Gram Specific Heat (Sgram):

$S_{g \mathrm{ram}}=\dfrac{Q}{\mathrm{~m} \Delta \mathrm{~T}}$

Relation between Gram and Molar Specific heat

$\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{mol}}=\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{w}} \mathrm{~S}_{\mathrm{} \mathrm{gram}}$

Heat Capacity: Heat capacity of a body is defined as the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of a given mass of a body by 1°C or 1K. It is also called thermal capacity.

$\text { Heat capacity }=\dfrac{Q}{\Delta T}$

Dimension :[ ML2 T–2K–1]

Latent Heat / Hidden Heat: Heat required to change the state of unit mass depends on the nature of substance and is called latent heat of substance.

$\mathrm{L}=\dfrac{\mathrm{Q}}{\mathrm{~m}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{mL}$

1. Latent heat of fusion: It is the quantity of heat (in kilocalories) required to change 1 kg mass of a substance from solid to liquid state at its melting point.

$\left[\mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{mL}_{\mathrm{f}}\right]$

$L_f \text { for } \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}=80 \frac{\mathrm{cal}}{\mathrm{gm}}$

2. Latent heat of vaporization :The quantity of heat required (in Kilocalories) to change its 1 kg mass from liquid to vapour state at its boiling point.

$\mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{mLv}$

$L_v \text { for } \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}=540 \frac{\mathrm{cal}}{\mathrm{gm}}$

Heating Curve

Heating of Solid: If to a given mass (m) of a solid, heat is supplied at constant rate and a graph is plotted between temperature and heat, as shown in figure, it is called heating curve.

Assumptions for heating curve:

1. Initially object is in solid state and its temperature is less then melting point

2. Heat is given to the system by a constant power source.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Calorimetry

Principle of calorimetry: When two bodies at different temperatures are mixed, heat will be transferred from body at higher temperature to a body at lower temperature till both acquire same temperature.

Heat Lost = Heat Gained (Principle of calorimetry)

Principle of calorimetry represents the law of conservation of heat energy.

Law of Mixtures

$\begin{aligned} & \text { Heat given = heat absorbed } \\ & \mathrm{m}_1 \mathrm{~s}_1 \Delta \mathrm{~T}_1=\mathrm{m}_2 \mathrm{~s}_2 \Delta \mathrm{~T}_2 \\ & \mathrm{~m}_1 \mathrm{~s}_1\left(\mathrm{~T}_1-\mathrm{T}_{\operatorname{mix}}\right)=\mathrm{m}_2 \mathrm{~s}_2\left(\mathrm{~T}_{\mathrm{mix}}-\mathrm{T}_2\right) \\ & (\mathrm{s}=\text { specific heat }) \\ & \left(\mathrm{T}_1>\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{mix}}>\mathrm{T}_2\right) \end{aligned}$

Note: The temperature of mixture can never be lesser than lower temperature (as a body cannot be cooled below the temperature of cooling body) and greater than higher temperature (as a body cannot be heated above the temperature of heating body).

Water Equivalent: The water equivalent of a body is the amount of water (W in gram) that absorbs or gives out the same amount of heat as is done by the body when heated or cooled through same temperature

$\begin{aligned} &\begin{aligned} & \left(\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{c}}\right)_{\text {substance }}=\left(\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{C}}\right)_{\text {water }} \\ & \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{s}} \mathrm{~S}_{\mathrm{s}}=\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{W}} \mathrm{~S}_{\mathrm{W}} \\ & \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{s}} \mathrm{~S}_{\mathrm{s}}=\mathrm{W} \times 1 \mathrm{cal} / \mathrm{g}^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \end{aligned}\\ &\text { Water Equivalent = W in gram } \end{aligned}$

Geyser Problem:

$\begin{aligned} \text { Power } & =\frac{\text { Work }}{\text { Time }} \\ \text { Power }(P) & =\frac{\text { Heat }}{\text { Time }}(\because \text { Heat }(Q)=m s \Delta T) \\ \frac{P}{4.2} & =\frac{m s \Delta T}{t} \\ P & =\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\sec } \text { or watt } \quad \frac{\mathrm{J}}{\sec (4.2)}=\frac{\mathrm{Cal}}{\mathrm{sec}} \\ \frac{P}{4.2} & =\left(\frac{m}{t}\right) s \Delta T \\ \left(\frac{m}{t}\right) & =\text { Rate of flow of water in } \frac{\mathrm{g}}{\mathrm{~s}} \\ S_{\text {water }} & =1 \frac{\text { cal }}{\mathrm{g}{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}} \end{aligned}$

Change of States:

1. Melting: Conversion of solid into liquid state at constant temperature is known as melting.

2.Boiling: Evaporation within the whole mass of the liquid is called boiling.

3.Evaporation: Conversion of liquid into vapours at all temperatures is called evaporation.

4.Heat of evaporation: Heat required to change unit mass of a liquid into vapour at a given temperature is called heat of evaporation at that temperature.

5.Sublimation: Direct conversion of solid into vapour state is called sublimation.

6.Heat of sublimation: Heat required to change unit mass of solid directly into vapours at a given temperature is called heat of sublimation at that temperature.

7.Condensation: The process of conversion from gaseous or vapour state to liquid state is known as condensation.

8.Hoar frost: Direct conversion of vapours into solid is called hoar frost. This process is just reverse of the process of sublimation.

Phase: The phase of a substance is defined as its form which is homogeneous, physically distinct and mechanically separable from the other forms of that substance.

Phase Diagram for Water: A phase diagram of water is a graph in which pressure (P) is represented along the y–axis and temperature (T) is represented along the x-axis.

$\text{As } \\ \text{Pressure } \uparrow \text{ MP } \downarrow \text{ BP } \uparrow \\ \text{Pressure } \downarrow \text{ MP } \uparrow \text{ BP } \downarrow$

Triple Point of Water and Regelation: The three curves in the phase diagram of water meet at a single point A, which is called the triple point of water.

Triple point of water represents a unique condition, and it is used to define the absolute temperature.

Regelation: It is the melting of ice caused by pressure and its re-solidification when the pressure is removed.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Modes of Heat Transfer: Heat is a form of energy which transfers from a body at higher temperature to a body at lower temperature. The transfer of heat from one body to another may take place by any one of the following modes.

1.Conduction: The process in which the material takes an active part by molecular action and energy is passed from one particle to another is called conduction. It is predominant in solids.

$\text { Rate of heat flow } i_T=\dfrac{d Q}{d t}=\dfrac{K A}{L}\left(T_1-T_2\right)$

1. Equivalent Thermal Conductivity in series Combination

$\begin{aligned} &\text { If lengths of rod is same then }\left(\mathrm{L}_1=\mathrm{L}_2=\mathrm{L}\right)\\ &\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{2 \mathrm{~K}_1 \mathrm{~K}_2}{\mathrm{~K}_1+\mathrm{K}_2} \end{aligned}$

$\displaystyle \begin{aligned} &\text { General formulae for series }\\ &K_{e 2}=\frac{l_1+l_2+\cdots}{\frac{l_1}{K_1}+\frac{l_2}{K_2}+\cdots} \end{aligned}$

2. Equivalent Thermal Conductivity in Parallel Combination

If Area of both rods are same then $ \left(\mathrm{A}_1=\mathrm{A}_2=\mathrm{A}\right)$

$\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{eq}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{K}_1+\mathrm{K}_2}{2}$

$\begin{aligned} &\text { General formulae for Parallel }\\ &k_{e q}=\frac{K_1 A_1+K_2 A_2+\cdots \cdot}{A_1+A_2+\cdots} \end{aligned}$

Temperature of junction: When we have to calculate the temperature of junction then we equate the rate of heat flow from both parts

$\mathrm{T}_0=\dfrac{\mathrm{K}_1 \mathrm{~L}_2 \mathrm{~T}_1+\mathrm{K}_2 \mathrm{~L}_1 \mathrm{~T}_2}{\mathrm{~K}_1 \mathrm{~L}_2+\mathrm{K}_2 \mathrm{~L}_1}$

Growth of Ice on Lake: time taken by ice to grow a thickness x is

$\mathrm{t}=\dfrac{\rho \mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{KT}} \int_0^{\mathrm{x}} \mathrm{xdx}=\dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{\rho \mathrm{~L}}{\mathrm{KT}} \mathrm{x}^2$

Time taken to double and triple the thickness ratio  $t_1: t_2: t_3:: 1^2: 2^2: 3^2$

Ratio of time taken to form thickness

$(0 \rightarrow \mathrm{x}):(\mathrm{x} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{x}):(2 \mathrm{x} \rightarrow 3 \mathrm{x})$

$\Delta \mathrm{t}_1: \Delta \mathrm{t}_2: \Delta \mathrm{t}_3:: \\ \left(\mathrm{x}^2-0^2\right):\left(2 \mathrm{x}^2-\mathrm{x}^2\right):\left(3 \mathrm{x}^2-2 \mathrm{x}^2\right)$

$\Delta \mathrm{t}_1: \Delta \mathrm{t}_2: \Delta \mathrm{t}_3: 1: 3: 5 $

2. Convection: The transfer of energy by actual motion of particle of medium from one place to another is called convection. It is predominant is fluids (liquids and gases).

• Reason for convection is difference in density due to heating
    • Direction of convection is bottoms to top due to gravity.

3. Radiation: Quickest way of transmission of heat is known as radiation. In this mode of energy transmission, heat is transferred from one place to another without effecting the intervening medium.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Prevost's Theory: According to Prevost's Theory, at every possible temperature (except zero kelvin temperature) there is a continuous heat energy exchange between a body and its surrounding and this exchange carry on for infinite time.

1.When a cold body is placed in the hot surrounding

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{B}}<\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{S}} \\ & \mathrm{Q}_{\text {emission }}<\mathrm{Q}_{\text {absorption }} \end{aligned}$

2.When a hot body placed in cooler surrounding

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{B}}>\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{S}} \\ & \mathrm{Q}_{\text {emission }}>\mathrm{Q}_{\text {absorption }} \end{aligned}$

3.When the temperature of a body is equal to the temperature of the surrounding

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{B}}=\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{S}} \\ & \mathrm{Q}_{\text {emission }}=\mathrm{Q}_{\text {absorotion }} \end{aligned}$

Absorptive power or absorptive coefficient (a) : The ratio of amount of radiation absorbed by a surface (Qa) to the amount of radiation incident (Q) upon it, is defined as the coefficient of absorption. It is unitless and dimensionless.

$a=\frac{Q_a}{Q} $

Spectral absorptive power:

$a_\lambda=\frac{Q_{a_\lambda}}{Q_\lambda}$

a= $\int_0^{\infty} \mathrm{a}_\lambda \mathrm{~d} \lambda $. For ideal black body  $ \mathrm{a}_{\lambda}$ and a=1, a and  $\mathrm{a}_{\lambda} $ are unitless

Emissive power (E):  The amount of heat radiation emitted by unit surface area in unit second at a particular temperature.

$E_{G B}=\frac{Q_{G B}}{A t} ; \quad E_{I B B}=\frac{Q_{I B B}}{A t}$

SI unit: J/m2–s or Watt/m2

Emissivity (e)

Absolute emissivity or emissivity: Radiation energy given out by a unit surface area of a body in unit time corresponding to unit temperature difference w.r.t. the surroundings is called Emissivity.

SI Unit:  W/m2

$\text { Relative emissivity ( } \left.e_r\right) \text { : } e_r=\frac{E_{G B}}{E_{I B B}}=\dfrac{\text { emitted radiation by gray body }\left(Q_{G B}\right)}{\text { emitted radiation by ideal bladk body }\left(Q_{I B B}\right)}$

GB = Gray or General body, IBB = Ideal black body

(1) Unitless

(2) For ideal black body ; er = 1

(3) range ; 0 < er < 1

Ideal Black Body: A body which absorbs all thermal radiations falling at its surface at low temperature and emits out all these absorbed radiations at high temperature, irrespective of their wave length is known as an ideal black body.

Kirchhoff's Law: At a given temperature for all bodies the ratio of their emissive power (E) to absorptive power (a) is constant and this constant is equal to emissive power (EiBB) of the ideal black body at same temperature.

$\dfrac{E_{\mathrm{GB}}}{\mathrm{a}}=\mathrm{E}_{I \mathrm{BB}}$

Good absorbers are Good emitters and Bad absorbers are Bad emitters.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Stefan's Law: The amount of radiation emitted per second per unit area (E) by ideal black body is directly proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature (T).

$\mathrm{E} \propto \mathrm{~T}^4 \Rightarrow \mathrm{E_{IBB}}=\sigma \mathrm{T}^4$

$E_{G B}=e_r \sigma T^4$

Newton's Law of Cooling: This law states that the rate of temperature change of an object is directly proportional to the difference in temperature between the object and its environment.

$-\frac{d T}{d t}=-k\left(T-T_{\mathrm{0}}\right)$

For Numerical Problems (Newton's Law of cooling)

$\left[\frac{\mathrm{T}_1-\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{t}}\right]=\mathrm{K}\left[\frac{\mathrm{~T}_1+\mathrm{T}_2}{2}-\mathrm{T}_0\right]$

Spectral Emissive Power : The amount of heat radiation emitted by unit area of the body in one second in unit spectral region at a given wavelength.

$\begin{array}{ll} \text { For } \mathrm{GB}, \mathrm{E}_\lambda=\frac{\left(\mathrm{Q}_{\lambda, \dot{A}}\right)_{\mathrm{GB}}}{\mathrm{At}} & \\ \text { For IBB, } \mathrm{E}_\lambda=\frac{\left(\mathrm{Q}_{\lambda \dot{A}}\right)_{\mathrm{IBB}}}{\mathrm{At}} \\ \text { UNIT : SI } \rightarrow \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^2-\AA \end{array}$

If the temperature of a black body is increased, the wavelength corresponding to maximum emission of radiation is shifted from longer wavelength to shorter wavelength, due to this colour of the body changes.

$\mathrm{T}_3>\mathrm{T}_2>\mathrm{T}_1 ; \lambda_{\mathrm{m}_3}<\lambda_{\mathrm{m}_2}<\lambda_{\mathrm{m}_1}$

Wein's Displacement Law: The wavelength (λm) corresponding to maximum emission of radiation decrease with increasing temperature. This is known as Wein’s displacement law.

$\lambda_{\mathrm{m}} \propto \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{~T}} \Rightarrow \lambda_{\mathrm{m}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{b}}{\mathrm{~T}}$

$\text { For numerical } \Rightarrow \lambda_{\mathrm{m}} \mathrm{~T}=\mathrm{b}$

$\text { (where, } \mathrm{b} \text { is Wein's constant }=2.89 \times 10^{-3}~ \mathrm{meter ~ Kelvin(mK)} \text { ) }$

$\lambda_{\mathrm{m}_1} \mathrm{~T}_1=\lambda_{\mathrm{m}_2} \mathrm{~T}_2$

Solar Constant: The Sun emits radiant energy continuously in space of which an in significant part reaches the Earth. The solar radiant energy received per unit area per unit time by a black surface held at right angles to the Sun's rays and placed at the mean distance of the Earth (in the absence of atmosphere) is called solar constant. The solar constant S is taken for earth to be 1340 watt/m2

$\left.\mathrm{S}=\dfrac{\sigma \mathrm{T}^2 \mathrm{R}^2}{\mathrm{~d}^2} \Rightarrow \mathrm{~S} \propto \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{~d}^2} \Rightarrow \dfrac{\mathrm{~S}_{\text {planet }}}{\mathrm{S}_{\text {earth }}}=\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{e}}}{\mathrm{~d}_{\mathrm{p}}}\right)^2 \right\rvert\,$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Kinetic Energy of Gas: All molecules of gas are continuously performing motion in random direction or say zig-zag direction. Apart from translational motion these molecules also perform rotational as well as vibrational motion. Thus, these molecules have kinetic energy associated with these motions. It is dependent on absolute temperature. Increasing temperature increases kinetic energy of gas.

Potential Energy: Intermolecular attraction force exists between molecules and thus every molecules have some potential energy.

Greater Intermolecular force (IMF), lesser will be potential energy and greater will be magnitude of potential energy

(1) Intermolecular force: Solid > Liquid > Gas (Real) > Ideal Gas (IMF = 0)

(2) Potential Energy: Solid < Liquid <= Gas (Real) < Ideal Gas (IMF = 0)

Internal Energy of Gas: Internal energy of gas is defined as sum of potential energy and kinetic energy at a temperature.

(1)Internal kinetic energy : Same for all

(2) Internal potential Energy : Maximum for ideal gas (PE = 0) and Minimum for solids (PE = negative)

(3)Internal Energy : Maximum for Ideal gas and Minimum for solid

Moles of gas ,$\mu=\frac{M}{M_w}=\frac{N}{N_A} \,$

Avogadro constant , $\mathrm{N}_A=6.023 \times 10^{23} \frac{\text { molecules }}{\text { mole }}$

Universal gas constant , $ \mathrm{R}=8.31 \frac{\mathrm{~J}}{\mathrm{~mole}-\mathrm{K}} \approx 2 \frac{\mathrm{cal}}{\mathrm{~mole}-\mathrm{K}}$

Specific gas constant , $ r=\frac{R}{M_w}$

Boltzmann constant , $ \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{b}}=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{~N}_{\mathrm{A}}}=1.38 \times 10^{-23} \frac{\mathrm{~J}}{\mathrm{~K}}$

Ideal Gas: A gas which follows all gas laws and gas equation at every possible temperature and pressure is known as ideal or perfect gas.

$\begin{aligned} & P V=\mu R T \\ & P V=\frac{M}{M_w} R T \quad \Rightarrow  P V=\left[\frac{m \mathrm{~N}}{\mathrm{mN}_{\mathrm{A}}}\right] \mathrm{RT} \\ & \mathrm{PV}=\left[\frac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{~N}_{\mathrm{A}}}\right] \mathrm{NT} \Rightarrow \mathrm{PV}=\mathrm{Nk}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{~T} \\ & \mathrm{P}=\frac{\rho \mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{W}}} \end{aligned}$

$\dfrac{P}{\rho}=\dfrac{R T}{M_w}=\dfrac{K_b T}{m}$

Gas Laws

1. Charle's Law:

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{V} \propto \mathrm{~T} \quad \text { (m and } \mathrm{P} \text { are Constant) } \\ & \frac{\mathrm{V}_1}{\mathrm{~V}_2}=\frac{\mathrm{T}_1}{\mathrm{~T}_2} \end{aligned}$

2. Boyle's Law:

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{V} \propto \frac{1}{\mathrm{P}} \quad \text { (m and } \mathrm{T} \text { are Constant) } \\ & \mathrm{P}_1 \mathrm{~V}_1=\mathrm{P}_2 \mathrm{~V}_2 \end{aligned}$

3. Gay–Lussac's Law:

$\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{P} \propto \mathrm{~T} \quad \text { ( } \mathrm{m} \text { and } \mathrm{V} \text { are Constant) }\\ &\frac{\mathrm{P}_1}{\mathrm{P}_2}=\frac{\mathrm{T}_1}{\mathrm{~T}_2} \end{aligned}$

4. Avogadro's Law: According to this law, at same temperature and pressure, equal volume of all gases contain equal number of molecules, i.e., N1 = N2 if P, V and T are same.

5. Dalton's Partial Pressure Mixture Law: According to this law, the pressure exerted by mixture of non-reactive gases is equal to the sum of partial pressure of each component gases present in the mixture.

$P=P_1+P_2+P_3 \ldots$

Partial pressure of gas 1

$P_1=\frac{\mu_1}{\mu_T} \times P_T$

Average velocity: Because molecules are in random motion in all possible direction with all possible velocity. Therefore, the average velocity of the gas molecules in container is zero.

$\langle\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}\rangle=\frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_1+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_2+\ldots \ldots \ldots . . . \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{N}}}{\mathrm{~N}}=0$

Average speed or Mean speed (vavg)

$<|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}|>\equiv \mathrm{v}_{\text {mean }} \equiv \mathrm{v}_{\text {avg }}=\frac{\left|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_1\right|+\left|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_2\right|+\ldots \ldots \ldots . .\left|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{n}}\right|}{\mathrm{N}}$

Most probable speed (vmp): At a given temperature, the speed to which maximum number of molecules belongs is called as most probable speed (vmp)

RMS Speed (vrms): RMS Speed (root mean squared speed) is equal to square root of the sum of square of speed of each molecule of a gas.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\mathrm{v}_1^2+\mathrm{v}_2^2+\mathrm{v}_3^2 \ldots \ldots \ldots \ldots+\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{n}}^2}{\mathrm{~N}}}$

blocks.text:
Maxwell's law of distribution of velocities :Maxwell had drawn a curve between number of molecules, moving with a particular velocity, and velocity of molecules known as velocity distribution curve.

Pressure of An Ideal gas:$P=\frac{1}{3} \rho v_{\mathrm{rms}}^2$

Translational Kinetic Energy:

​$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{T}}=\frac{3}{2} \mathrm{PV}=\frac{1}{2} m_{\text {total }} v_{\text {rms }}^2 \\ & \frac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{T}}}{\mathrm{~V}}=\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{V}}=\text { Energy density } \\ & \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{V}}=\frac{3}{2} \mathrm{P} \end{aligned}$

Expression of RMS Speed

$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{P}}{\rho}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{w}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{~m}}}$

(1)If gas is same ($M_w = \text{const.}$) and temp. is changed

$V_{\text{rms}} \propto \sqrt{T}$

(2) If temperature is constant and gas is changed

$V_{\text{rms}} \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{M_w}}$

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{P}}{\rho}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{w}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{~m}}}$

$v_{\mathrm{mp}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{P}}{\rho}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{w}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{~m}}}$

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{av}}=\sqrt{\frac{8 \mathrm{P}}{\pi \rho}}=\sqrt{\frac{8 \mathrm{RT}}{\pi \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{w}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{8 \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{~T}}{\pi \mathrm{~m}}}$

$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{rms}}>\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{Mean}}>\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{MP}}$

(3) If pressure changed at constant temp. No effect on  $V_{rms}$ .

(4) $V_{rms}$ doesn't depend on pressure but pressure depends on  $V_{rms}$ .

Escape Velocity: The minimum velocity required for which molecule or object to escape out from earth surface.

$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{es}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{GM}}{\mathrm{R}}} \\  \Rightarrow \left(\mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{es}}\right)_{\mathrm{earth}}=11.2 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{sec}$

Relation of escape Velocity with rms

Condition for atmosphere to be present at the surface of any planet:

Vrms < Ves $\rightarrow$Atmosphere present

Vrms ≥ Ves $\rightarrow$ No atmosphere

$\mathrm{T}_{\min }=\dfrac{\left(\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{es}}\right)^2 \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{w}}}{3 \mathrm{R}} \quad \text{OR } \quad T_{\text {min }}=\dfrac{M_w}{2} \times 10^7 \mathrm{~K}$  $(M_w ~ in~ Kg)$

Note:

(1)   If we continuously increase the temperature at 104 K hydrogen gas molecules will leave the earth surface first.

(2) Moon has no atmosphere because there rms speed of gas molecules is greater then the escape velocity.

blocks.text:
Degrees of Freedom (f): The number of independent ways in which a molecule or an atom can exhibit motion or have energy is called its degrees of freedom.

Types of Degrees of freedom:

(a) Translational Degree of freedom : Number of independent ways in which a gas molecule may perform translatory motion. There are maximum three degree of freedom corresponding to translational motion.

(b) Rotational Degree of freedom : Number of independent ways in which a gas molecule may perform rotational motion. The number of degrees of freedom in this case depends on the structure of the molecule.

(c) Vibrational Degree of freedom : Number of independent ways in which a gas molecule may vibrate. It is exhibited at high temperature only.

Maxwell's Law of Equipartition of Energy: The total kinetic energy of a gas molecules is equally distributed among its all degree of freedom and the energy associated with each degree of freedom at absolute temperature T is $\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{~T}$

Mayer’s Law:

$C_p-C_v=R$

$\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{v}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{f}}{2} \mathrm{R} ; \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{p}}=\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{f}}{2}+1\right) \mathrm{R}$

Molar specific heat for mixture of gases:

$Q_{\text {mix }}=Q_1+Q_2$

$C_{\operatorname{mix}}=\dfrac{\mu_1 C_1+\mu_2 C_2}{\mu_1+\mu_2}$

$\left(\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{V}}\right)_{\text {mix }}=\dfrac{\mu_1 \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{v}_1}+\mu_2 \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{V}_2}}{\mu_1+\mu_2}$

$\left(\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{P}}\right)_{\text {mix }}=\dfrac{\mu_1 \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{P}_1}+\mu_2 \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{P}_2}}{\mu_1+\mu_2}$

$\gamma_{\text {mix }}=\dfrac{\mu_1 C_{p_1}+\mu_2 C_{P_2}}{\mu_1 C_{v_1}+\mu_2 C_{V_2}}$

Mixture of Gases

Case – I: Here two gases kept in two different vessels are mixed in another vessel

$\dfrac{P_1 V_1}{T_1}+\dfrac{P_2 V_2}{T_2}=\dfrac{P_3 V_3}{T_3}$

Case – II: Here two gases kept in two different vessels connected via a tube as shown. Cross-section area of this tube is very small so its volume can be neglected w.r.t. volume of vessel

$\dfrac{\mathrm{P}_1 \mathrm{~V}_1}{\mathrm{~T}_1}+\dfrac{\mathrm{P}_2 \mathrm{~V}_2}{\mathrm{~T}_2}=\dfrac{P V_1}{\mathrm{~T}_1^{\prime}}+\dfrac{\mathrm{PV}_2}{\mathrm{~T}_2^{\prime}}$

Mean Free Path: The average distance travelled by a molecule between two successive collisions is called as mean free path  of the molecule.

$ \lambda_{\mathrm{m}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2} \pi \mathrm{~d}^2 \mathrm{n}} $

Here,

$ \mathrm{n}  =\dfrac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{~V}}= $ No. of molecules per unit volume

$ \mathrm{d}  =\text { diameter of a molecule } $

Compressibility Factor: It is used to express the extent of deviation of a real gas from ideal gas behaviour. It is denoted by Z.

Case-I :         Z = 1      $\Rightarrow$           [Vreal = Videal]

Thus, real gas behaves as ideal gas (zero deviation).

Case-II :         Z > 1     $\Rightarrow$          [Vreal > Videal]

Thus, real gas expand with respect to ideal gas and hence we can say positive deviation.

Case-III :       Z < 1       $\Rightarrow$         [Vreal < Videal]

Thus, real gas compress with respect to ideal gas and hence we can say negative deviation.

Real Gas : Practically, no gas is ideal at all. They show some deviation from ideal gas behaviour and are known as Real gas.

Main cause of deviation is two postulates that have been assumed in Kinetic Theory of Gases :-

(1) Interaction force between gas molecules are considered negligible

(2) Size of Gas molecules is considered negligible but practically they are not negligible.

Compressibility Factor Curve:

NOTE: Real gas approaches ideal gas behaviour at Low Pressure and High Temperature(Low Density).

Vander Waal's Equation for Real Gas

Pressure Correction: Since, we have neglected intermolecular interaction, thus actual pressure of gas will be less than ideal pressure.

$P_{\text {ideal }}=P_{\text {real }}+\dfrac{\mu^2 a}{V^2}$

Volume Correction: Also, we have neglected size of molecules but actual volume occupied by real gas will be

$\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{V}_{\text {ideal }}=\mathrm{V}_{\text {real }}-\mu \mathrm{b}\\ &\mathrm{b} \rightarrow \text { Constant and value depends on real gas} \end{aligned}$

$\left(P+\dfrac{\mu^2 a}{V^2}\right)(V-\mu b)=\mu R T $

Process: When a system changes from one equilibrium state to another, the path of successive states through which the system passes is called a process.

  • Cyclic Process-It is a thermodynamic process in which the system returns to its initial stage after undergoing a series of changes.
  • Non–cyclic process-It is a process in which the system does not return to its initial stage.
  • Quasi–static or equilibrium process-It A thermodynamic process that occurs very slowly, ensuring that at every moment, the temperature and pressure remain uniform throughout the system, is referred to as a quasi-static process..
First Law of Thermodynamics(FLOT): Suppose some heat is supplied to a system capable of doing external work. In that case, the heat absorbed by the system is equivalent to the combined effect of the increase in its internal energy and the external work it executes.

$\Delta Q=\Delta U+\Delta \mathrm{W}$

  • Mathematical Method $\mathrm{W}=\int_{V_i}^{V_f} P d V$
  • Cyclic Process-:Work =Area of the closed curve in PV Graph
  • Isochoric Process :Work =0
  • Isothermal Process: $\text { Work }=\mu R T \log _e\left[\frac{V_f}{V_i}\right]=\mu R T \log _e\left[\frac{P_i}{P_f}\right]$
  • Adiabatic Process :$\text { Work }=\mu R \frac{\left(T_f-T_i\right)}{1-\gamma}$
  • Isobaric Process:$\text { Work= } \mathrm{P}\left(V_f-V_i\right)=\mu R\left(T_f-T_i\right) \mid$
6.  Polytropic Process:$\text { Work }=\dfrac{\mu R\left(T_f-T_i\right)}{1-x}$

Graphical method $\Delta \mathbf{W}$= Area enclosed between PV curve and Volume axis.

Cyclic Process: A cyclic process in thermodynamics refers to a process in which a system undergoes a series of changes but eventually returns to its original state.

1. Isometric or Isochoric Process: Isochoric process is a thermodynamic process that takes place at constant volume of the system, but pressure and temperature varies for change in state of the system.

Volume= Constant

$\text { Equation of state } \Rightarrow \frac{P}{T}=\text { constant }$

$\text { Work done } \mathrm{W}=\int P d V=0 \quad(: \mathrm{dV}=0)$

$\text { Form of First Law }, \mathrm{Q}=\Delta U=\mu C_v \Delta T$

$\text { Slope of the P-V curve } \dfrac{d P}{d V}=\infty$

$\text { Bulk Modulus }=\beta=-\frac{d P}{d V / v}=-v \frac{d P}{d v}=\infty$

2. Isobaric Process: Isobaric process is a thermodynamic process that takes place at constant pressure, but volume and temperature varies for change in state of the system.

Pressure = constant

$\displaystyle \text { Equation of state } \Rightarrow \frac{V}{T}=\text { constant }(\mathrm{V} \propto \mathrm{~T})$

$\displaystyle \text { Work done } \mathrm{}=\mathrm{W}=\int_{V_i}^{V_f} P d V=\mathrm{P}\left(V_f-V_i\right)$

From the FLOT : $\Delta Q=\Delta U+W$

$\mu~C_p\left(T_f-T_i\right)=\mu C_v\left(T_f-T_i\right)+\mathrm{P}\left(V_f-V_i\right)$

$\text { Slope of the PV curve }\left(\dfrac{d P}{d V}\right)_{\text {isobaric }}=0$

$\text{Bulk Modulus  } \beta_{IB}=0 $

3. Isothermal Process: In this process pressure and volume of system change but temperature remains constant.

Temperature= constant

Equation of state PV=Constant

$\text { Work done } \mathrm{W}=\mu R T \log _e\left[\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}\right\rfloor=2.303 \mu R T \log _{10}\left\lfloor\dfrac{P_1}{P_2}\right\rfloor$

$\text { Form of First Law } \Delta U=0$ so that $\Delta Q=W_{\text {isothermal }}$

$\text { Slope of isothermal curve } \left.\left[\dfrac{d P}{d V}\right]_{\text {isothermal }}=-\dfrac{P}{V}\right\rfloor$

Bulk modulus ${\beta _{IT}} = P$

4. Adiabatic Process: It is that thermodynamic process in which pressure, volume and temperature of the system do change but there is no exchange of heat between the system and the surroundings.

$\text{Adiabatic equation on of state} \\  \begin{aligned} & P V^\gamma=C \\ & T V^{\gamma-1}=C \\ & T^\gamma P^{1-\gamma}=C \end{aligned}$

No heat exchange between system and surroundings.

$\text { Work done } \mathrm{W}=\dfrac{1}{\gamma-1}\left[P_1 V_1-P_2 V_2\right]=\dfrac{\mu R}{\gamma-1}\left(T_1-T_2\right)$

$\text { Slope of adiabatic curve }\left[\dfrac{d P}{d V}\right]_{\text {adiabatic }}=\dfrac{-\Upsilon P}{V}$

$\text{Bulk Modulus } =\beta_{A D}=\gamma P$

5.Polytropic Process

$\mathrm{P} V^x=\text { Constant }, \mathrm{C}=C_v+\dfrac{R}{1-x}$

$\text { For isobaric } \mathrm{x}=0, \mathrm{C}=C_P=\dfrac{R}{\gamma-1}+\mathrm{R}=C_v+R$

$\text { For isothermal } x=1, C=\infty$

$\text { For adiabatic } x=\gamma, C=0$
